text: For hundreds of millions of years, the rules of the pond seemed simple.
nxt: If you are an amphibian with a lightning-fast tongue, insects are food.

title: The Rule of the Pond
text: Imagine a damp bank near a shallow pool, late at night. A frog sits very still, watching for movement.

title: The Rule of the Pond
text: A few inches away, something small and pale is twitching. It looks soft, slow, and defenseless.
nxt: To the frog, it looks like the easiest meal of the week.

title: Meet Epomis
text: Meet Epomis, a genus of ground beetles. Ground beetles are common night hunters.
nxt: They run across soil and leaf litter, and most of them eat small prey like worms, snails, or caterpillars.

title: Meet Epomis
text: They called it a role reversal: the animal that should be the predator becomes the prey.

title: A Frog's Eyes
text: To see how this works, we first have to understand a frog's eyes. A frog does not look at the world the way you do.

title: A Frog's Eyes
text: Its visual system is tuned to catch small moving things.
nxt: A tiny dark spot that twitches is a signal that says, strike now.

title: A Frog's Eyes

title: A Frog's Eyes
text: This reflex has fed frogs for a very long time. Epomis has learned to push exactly that button.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: When a frog comes near, the larva does not hide, and it does not run.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: It stays still and starts to move its antennae and its jaws, in a slow rhythm, up and down and from side to side.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: To us it might look like a tiny dance. To a frog, it can look like a worm, wriggling on the ground.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: The researchers counted the movements.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: The larva was not just wiggling. It was paying attention.
nxt: That control matters, because it shows that the dance is not random shaking.

title: The Dancing Lure
text: It changes with the distance to the victim. A trap that gets more convincing as the target gets closer is a very clever trap.

title: The Strike
text: Now the frog commits. It turns its body toward the larva, lowers its head, and creeps closer. The larva does not flinch.

title: The Strike
text: It keeps waving. Then the frog strikes.
nxt: A frog's tongue can leave its mouth in a fraction of a second, far too fast for you to follow with your eyes.

title: The Strike
text: For almost any insect, this is the end.
nxt: The tongue is wet and sticky, it snaps back with the prey stuck on it, and the meal is swallowed before the insect understands what happened.

title: The Strike
text: A frog that uses this weapon again and again rarely misses a small, wriggling target.
nxt: That is exactly why the larva's trick is so shocking: it survives the one move that almost always works.

title: The Strike
text: But in the Epomis experiments, the larva usually avoids the tongue. The authors write that it almost always dodges the strike.

title: The Strike
text: Then it does something no ordinary insect would dare.
nxt: It uses the moment, when the frog is open and close, to grab on to the amphibian's body with its hooked jaws.

title: The Hooked Jaws
text: Look closely at those jaws. They are long, curved, and sharp. Once they sink in, they are very hard to pull out.

title: The Hooked Jaws
text: The frog shakes its head. It kicks and scrapes at its own skin.
nxt: But the larva is small, and it is holding on at a place the frog cannot easily reach.

title: Swallowed Alive?
text: What does the frog do when it cannot get rid of its attacker? In some cases, it swallows the larva.

title: Swallowed Alive?
text: In seven of the trials, the amphibian gulped the larva down and later spat it back out, alive.

title: Swallowed Alive?
text: In one case, a young toad kept a larva in its stomach for about two hours before it came back up.

title: Swallowed Alive?
text: The larva then simply attached itself to the skin of the animal that had swallowed it.
nxt: The usual rule of the food chain had failed, again.

title: The Experiment
text: Here is what the experiments showed.

title: The Experiment
text: One detail matters. The amphibians were young, only two to three weeks after metamorphosis. So these were not giant frogs.

title: The Experiment
text: They were small, but still much bigger than the larvae that beat them.
nxt: In about seventy percent of those encounters, the larva lured the amphibian before it attacked, and the amphibian was eaten.

title: The Experiment

title: The Experiment
text: In the rest, the meeting was accidental, with no luring, but it still ended badly for the amphibian.

title: The Experiment
text: Across the study, the authors report a success rate of close to one hundred percent for the larvae.

title: Feeding
text: What happens after the jaws bite? Like many ground beetle larvae, Epomis feeds in a way that sounds strange.

title: Feeding
text: It cannot swallow chunks of meat. So it first sucks out the body fluids of its victim, and later it chews.

title: Feeding
text: The press coverage of the study describes a slow process.
nxt: In the end, the researchers report that all that remains of the amphibian is a pile of bones.

title: Feeding
text: The slow part matters. Ground beetle larvae often use digestive fluids to soften their food before they take it in.

title: Feeding
text: That lets a tiny animal eat something far larger than its own mouth.

title: Feeding
text: A larva can stay fixed to one spot on its host, feed, and grow, while the amphibian can do nothing about it.

title: Three Stages
text: What we do know is that this larva has three stages. At the end of each stage, it drops off its host and molts in a hidden place.

title: Three Stages
text: Each new stage needs a new meal.

title: Three Stages
text: That is a lot of victims for something so small.

title: Becoming an Adult
text: After the third stage, the larva digs into the soil and builds a small chamber. Inside, in the dark, it changes.

title: Becoming an Adult
text: Its body is taken apart and rebuilt.
nxt: Weeks later, an adult beetle comes out, with a hard shell and long legs, ready to run across the ground at night.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: You might expect the adult to move on to an easier diet. Instead, the adult is also a hunter of amphibians.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: The study describes adults as generalist predators that eat many kinds of food, including amphibians.
nxt: So we cannot say that adult Epomis eat only frogs.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: What we can say is that they do attack them.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: In the laboratory, the researchers saw an adult jump onto the back of an amphibian.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: It used its jaws to make a cut in the back, and the victim became paralyzed within a few minutes.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: Within hours, the adult had eaten most of its prey, working from the legs up, until only a head and limbs were left.

title: The Adult Hunter
text: These details come from reports on the study, and the authors describe adult hunting as early-stage research.

title: In the Wild
text: The wild observations are even more interesting. Wizen and Gasith found three adult beetles in the wild that were eating toads from behind.

title: In the Wild
text: That fits what we saw in the lab. But three beetles is a small sample.
nxt: Nobody can yet say how often adults do this outside the laboratory, or exactly how the bite works.

title: The Toad Poison Puzzle
text: What about the poison in toads? Many toads carry defensive chemicals in their skin. It would be tempting to say that Epomis is immune.

title: The Toad Poison Puzzle
text: But the original paper does not report on toxin tests. So the honest answer is that we do not know how these beetles deal with toad poison.
nxt: No one has solved that puzzle yet.

title: Why Evolve This?
text: Why would a beetle ever evolve such a bold strategy? Scientists suspect it started as a defense.

title: Why Evolve This?
text: If a larva lives where amphibians hunt, the ones that learned to dodge a tongue and bite back would survive.

title: Why Evolve This?
text: Over a long time, defense could turn into attack. This is a hypothesis. It is a reasonable one, but it is not a proven history.

title: The Red Queen
text: There is also a bigger idea behind this story. Biologists sometimes talk about the Red Queen hypothesis.

title: The Red Queen
text: It says that living things keep changing just to keep up with each other, like runners on a treadmill.

title: The Red Queen
text: A frog's hunting reflex works well against most insects. That makes the one insect that can beat it very unusual, and very interesting.

title: The Reflex Trap
text: The frog's weakness is also its strength.
nxt: The reflex that finds food quickly cannot easily stop to ask whether the target is a worm or a trap.

title: The Reflex Trap
text: The reflex that finds food quickly cannot easily stop to ask whether the target is a worm or a trap.

title: The Reflex Trap
text: The same speed that makes frogs good hunters makes them easy to fool. Epomis does not beat the reflex with strength.

title: The Reflex Trap
text: It beats it with timing and a clever disguise.

title: Where They Live
text: Where do these beetles live? The study was done in Israel, on two species, Epomis circumscriptus and Epomis dejeani.

title: Where They Live
text: Other species in the genus have been reported in other parts of the Old World, including Africa and Asia.

title: Where They Live
text: The same paper points to older reports of another species, Epomis nigricans, feeding on amphibians in Japan and in Sri Lanka.

title: Where They Live
text: So this habit is not a one-country curiosity.
nxt: But the wild lives of most of these beetles are poorly known, which is part of why Epomis still surprises scientists.

title: Hidden at Night
text: It also reminds us how little we see at night. These beetles are small, they hide in shelters during the day, and they hunt in the dark.

title: Hidden at Night
text: Amphibians use the same damp hiding places, under stones and old wood.

title: The Whole Story
text: Let us put the whole story together. A larva waits in the dark and waves its antennae. A young amphibian sees a worm and strikes.

title: The Whole Story
text: The larva slips the tongue and bites on. It feeds, drops off, molts, and does it again.
nxt: Later it becomes an adult that can ambush an amphibian by jumping onto its back.

title: The Whole Story
text: At no point in this chain is the beetle stronger than its prey. It is simply better prepared.

title: A Pond at Night
text: So the next time you stand beside a quiet pond on a warm evening, listen to the frogs.

title: A Pond at Night
text: Under the sound is a tiny, patient drama.

title: A Lesson About Size
text: It is a lesson about size. We assume that bigger animals always win, and that a backbone beats a bug.

title: A Lesson About Size
text: Nature does not care about our rankings. Given enough time, evolution can find a way to turn almost any strength into a weakness.

title: A Lesson About Size
text: Which other hunters are hiding a trick we have not noticed yet?
